drug_class: Type I interferon receptor antagonist (a targeted biologic medication)
purpose: Anifrolumab-fnia is used to treat moderate to severe systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which is commonly known as lupus. It is used in adults who are already taking other lupus medicines but still need more help controlling their disease. It can help reduce lupus flares and ease symptoms like joint pain, skin rashes, and fatigue.
how_it_works: In people with lupus, the immune system is overactive and attacks the body's own tissues. A group of proteins called type I interferons play a big role in driving this overactivity. Anifrolumab works by blocking the receptor that these interferons attach to, which helps calm down the overactive immune response and reduce inflammation and damage throughout the body.
common_side_effects: Upper respiratory infections (like a cold or sore throat), bronchitis, infusion-related reactions (such as headache, nausea, dizziness, or flushing during or after the IV infusion), shingles (herpes zoster), and back pain.
warnings: Because this medicine lowers your immune system's activity, you are at a higher risk of getting infections, including serious ones. Tell your doctor right away if you develop signs of infection like fever, chills, or cough. There is also an increased risk of shingles, so talk to your doctor about getting vaccinated before starting treatment. Do not use this medication if you have an active serious infection. Live vaccines should be avoided while on this medicine. It is given as an IV infusion in a clinic, so you will be monitored for infusion reactions.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 300 mg given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into a vein over about 30 minutes. It is given once every 4 weeks by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting. You should continue taking your other lupus medications unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
